results.summary_before: This design shows two animations on a 7-segment display: alternating letters F and H, or a rotation animation. It divides a 10 kHz clock input based on input 7 and uses input 0 to select the mode, input 1 for blinking the dot, input 5 to pause, and input 6 for debug. Testing requires applying a 10 kHz clock and observing the display; silicon tests confirm it works correctly. The project was created during the Hackaday Conference 2024.

results.summary_before: This design implements an even and odd BCD counter that can be selected via two inputs. When input 1 is high, the even counter is active; when input 2 is high, the odd counter is active. The outputs are 7-bit BCD values intended to drive a 7-segment display. Testing involves setting the inputs and observing the count on a connected 7-segment display.

results.summary_before: This is a configurable digital clock that defaults to 20 MHz but can be set to 10, 12, or 14 MHz via input pins. It supports display of minutes or hours on a 2-digit 7-segment display, with an option for 4-digit mode, and includes an Arduino mode. External hardware includes a PMOD 2-segment display (and possibly a 4-segment display). The design is simple and intended for basic timekeeping with adjustable speed for setting.

results.summary_before: This project runs the main peripherals of a Basys 3 FPGA board over a 115200 baud UART link. It handles 16 LED inputs, 16 switch outputs, 12 seven-segment display inputs, and 5 button outputs, all communicated via UART TX and RX routed to the bidirectional PMOD bus. Testing can be done with an associated PMOD board or by interacting with the UART, expecting messages like "LD: 0xFFFF" and "SW: 0xFFFF". The design enables remote control of Basys 3 peripherals through a serial connection.
